title: Is leaking urine just a normal part of getting older or having kids?
d: It's common, but it isn't something you have to accept. Leaking after childbirth or around menopause often improves with pelvic floor physical therapy, which guidelines recommend as a first treatment for stress and mixed incontinence in women.

title: Aren't Kegels enough?
d: Sometimes, if they're done correctly and they match your problem. Many women squeeze the wrong muscles or hold their breath, and some have pelvic floor muscles that are already too tight, where more squeezing can make symptoms worse. A pelvic floor evaluation shows which approach you need.

title: How long does it take to see results?

title: When should I start physical therapy after a car accident?
d: Once a doctor has ruled out a serious injury such as a fracture, starting guided movement and exercise sooner is generally better than waiting for the pain to go away on its own.

d: For whiplash without a fracture, guidelines generally advise against a soft collar. Gentle movement helps recovery more than keeping the neck still.

title: Why did my pain start a day or two after the accident?

title: Do I need surgery for carpal tunnel?
d: Not usually for mild to moderate symptoms. Splinting, activity changes and physical therapy help many people. Constant numbness or thumb muscle weakness usually needs a hand specialist, and surgery is sometimes the best option.

title: How long does tennis elbow take to heal?
d: Tendon pain improves gradually, over weeks to months. A structured strengthening program usually shortens the road, and your therapist will adjust it as you improve.

title: Should I wear an elbow brace?
d: A forearm strap can ease pain in the short term for some people. It works best alongside strengthening exercise, not instead of it.

title: Do I have to stop working or playing?
d: Usually not completely. We change how you grip and how much you do so the tendon can recover while you stay active.

title: I don't play tennis. Can I still have tennis elbow?
d: Yes. Most people with tennis elbow don't play tennis. Gripping at work, tools, computer use and yard work are more common causes.

title: Can a physical therapist treat TMJ?
d: Yes. Physical therapists treat jaw pain with hands-on techniques, jaw and neck exercises, and habit changes. Conservative treatments like these are the recommended starting point for most TMJ disorders.

title: Do I need to see a dentist first?
d: Not to start physical therapy. If you have tooth pain, a change in your bite, or you grind your teeth at night, a dentist should check you as well, and we can work alongside them.

title: Will I need a mouth guard?
d: That's a decision for your dentist. Many people get relief from physical therapy and habit changes, with or without a guard.

title: Can TMJ cause headaches?
d: Yes. Tight chewing muscles and jaw problems often cause headaches around the temples, and neck tension can add to them. Treating the jaw and neck together often helps both.

x: Conditions We Treat / Vertigo & Dizziness Dizziness & Balance Vertigo and Dizziness (BPPV) Treatment in Bakersfield If the room spins for a few seconds when you roll over in bed, lie down or look up, you may have BPPV, the most common cause of vertigo. It's usually very treatable with physical therapy, often in just a few visits. Request an Evaluation Yes, physical therapy can treat vertigo caused by BPPV. BPPV happens when tiny calcium crystals in the inner ear drift into the wrong place, so certain head movements set off a brief, intense spinning feeling. The clinical practice guideline from the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery recommends repositioning maneuvers, such as the Epley maneuver, to move the crystals back. A trained physical therapist can find which ear and which canal is involved and treat it, and many people feel much better within one to three treatments. title: Can a physical therapist really fix vertigo?
d: For BPPV, often yes. BPPV is caused by inner-ear crystals out of place, and repositioning maneuvers performed by a trained physical therapist move them back. Many people feel much better within one to three treatments.

title: Is this the same as the Epley maneuver I saw online?
d: The Epley maneuver is one of the repositioning treatments. It only works for BPPV in one particular canal, on the correct side. An evaluation identifies which ear and which canal is involved, so the right maneuver is used.

title: Will the treatment make me dizzy?
d: It can, briefly. The testing and the maneuver may bring on the spinning for a few seconds, which is expected. Your therapist stays with you and moves at your pace.

title: Can vertigo come back?
d: BPPV can return, sometimes months or years later. The good news is that it usually responds to the same treatment again, and your therapist can show you what to watch for.

title: Sciatica and back pain
d: Pain that runs from your low back into your buttock or leg, often from an irritated disc or nerve, or stiffness and aching in the back itself. Most people improve without surgery, and specific exercise and hands-on care are the recommended first step.

title: Headaches that start in the neck
d: Headaches that begin at the base of the skull or on one side of the head, often worse with certain neck positions or long hours at a desk. Hands-on treatment for the neck and targeted strengthening can reduce how often they come and how bad they get. A sudden, severe or “worst ever” headache needs a doctor right away.

title: Neck pain and whiplash after a car accident
d: Neck pain, stiffness and headaches after a car accident can show up hours or days later. Once a doctor has ruled out a serious injury, gentle movement, hands-on care and progressive exercise help you recover and get back to normal activity. If you have severe neck pain, numbness or weakness after a crash, get checked by a doctor first.

title: Frozen shoulder and rotator cuff pain
d: Pain reaching overhead or behind your back, pain lying on that side at night, or a shoulder that has slowly stiffened. Physical therapy restores motion first, then rebuilds strength, and most rotator cuff and frozen shoulder problems improve without surgery.

title: Tennis elbow and golfer’s elbow
d: Pain on the outside (tennis) or inside (golfer’s) of the elbow, worse with gripping, lifting or typing, and you don't have to play either sport to get it. Progressive tendon-strengthening exercise, changes to how you grip and work, and hands-on care are the mainstays of treatment.

title: Carpal tunnel and hand numbness
d: Numbness or tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, often worse at night, driving or typing. For mild to moderate symptoms, physical therapy with nerve and tendon gliding exercises, splinting advice and changes to how you use your hands can help. Constant numbness or hand weakness should be checked by a doctor.

title: Knee arthritis and knee pain
d: Pain on stairs, stiffness after sitting, or a knee that swells after a busy day. Exercise-based physical therapy is one of the most strongly recommended treatments for knee osteoarthritis, and for some people it can put off the need for surgery.

title: Plantar fasciitis and heel pain
d: Sharp pain in the bottom of your heel with your first steps in the morning or after sitting. Hands-on therapy, stretching, taping, strengthening and footwear advice treat it without injections or surgery for most people.

title: Bladder leaks (urinary incontinence)
d: Leaking when you cough, sneeze, laugh, lift or exercise, or sudden urges you can't hold. Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is recommended as a first treatment for stress and mixed incontinence in women, before medication or surgery.

title: Pelvic organ prolapse
d: A feeling of heaviness, pressure or bulging in the vagina, often after childbirth or menopause and worse at the end of the day. Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is recommended for symptoms of mild to moderate prolapse, along with lifting and bowel habits that reduce strain.

title: Pelvic pain and painful sex
d: Pain with intercourse, pelvic or tailbone pain, or pain with tampons or exams is often linked to pelvic floor muscles that are tight or overworked. Pelvic floor therapy helps these muscles relax and work properly, gently and at your pace, in a private room.

title: Diastasis recti (separated abdominal muscles)
d: A gap or bulge down the middle of your belly after pregnancy, sometimes with low back pain or a “pooch” that exercise hasn't fixed. Physical therapy retrains your deep core and pelvic floor to work together so you can return to exercise with confidence.

title: Vertigo and dizziness (BPPV)
d: The room spins for a few seconds when you roll over in bed, lie down or look up. This is often BPPV, the most common cause of vertigo, and repositioning treatment by a trained physical therapist often helps within a few visits.

title: TMJ and jaw pain
d: Aching in the jaw or temples, painful clicking, trouble opening wide, or clenching and grinding. Gentle hands-on care, jaw and neck exercises and habit changes are an effective first treatment for most TMJ problems.

title: Osteoporosis and bone health
d: If you've been told you have osteopenia or osteoporosis, the right exercise matters. Physical therapy teaches safe strengthening and weight-bearing exercise, balance training to lower your risk of falls, and ways to move that protect your spine.

title: Getting stronger before surgery (prehab)
d: Building strength and motion before a planned knee, hip or shoulder surgery, learning the exercises you'll use afterward, and preparing your home and routine, so recovery starts on a better footing.

title: Recovery after surgery
d: Rehabilitation after joint replacement, ACL and rotator cuff repair, spine surgery and more, coordinated with your surgeon's protocol.
